source_text: Paulus vero Apostolus de persecutore, qui primus Ecclesiae sanguinem fudit, postea gladium stylo mutans, et convertens machaeram in aratrum; lupus rapax Benjamin, dehinc ipse afferens escam secundum Jacob, qualiter martyria, jam et sibi optabilia, commendat! cum de Thessalonicensibus gaudens: Uti, inquit, gloriemur in vobis in Ecclesiis Dei pro tolerantia vestra et fide, in omnibus persecutionibus et pressuris, quibus sustinetis ostentamen justi judicii Dei, ut digni habeamini regno ejus, pro quo et patimini. Sicut et ad Romanos: Non solum autem, verum etiam exultantes in pressuris; certi quod pressura tolerantiam perficit, tolerantia vero probationem, probatio autem spem, spes vero non confundit. Et rursus: Quod si filii, et haeredes; haeredes quidem Dei, cohaeredes vero Christi: siquidem compatimur, uti et cum illo glorificemur. Reputo enim passiones hujus temporis non esse dignas ad gloriam, quae in nobis revelabitur. Et ideo postmodum: Quis, inquit, separabit nos a dilectione Christi? pressura, an angustia, an fames, an nuditas, an periculum, an machaera, secundum quod scriptum est: tui caussa mortificamur tota die, deputati sumus ut pecora jugulationis; sed in omnibus istis supervincimus pro eo qui nos dilexit. Persuasum enim habemus, quod neque mors, neque vita, neque virtus, neque sublimitas, neque profundum, neque alia conditio poterit nos a dilectione Dei separare, quae est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro. Sed et Corinthiis passiones suas enumerans, patiendum utique praefinivit: In laboribus abundantius, in carceribus plurimum, in mortibus saepius; a Judaeis quinquies quadragenas citra unam accepi, ter virgis caesus, semel lapidatus, et reliqua. Quae si magis incommoda quam martyria videbuntur, tamen rursus: Propter quod, inquit, boni duco in infirmitatibus, in injuriis, in necessitatibus, in persecutionibus, in angustiis pro Christo. Etiam in superioribus: Qui in omnibus tribulemur, sed non coangustemur; et indigeamus, sed non perindigeamus; quoniam persecutionibus agitemur, sed non derelinquamur; qui dejiciamur, sed non pereamus: semper mortificationem Christi Jesu in corpore nostro circumferentes. Sed etsi, inquit, exterior homo noster vitiatur, caro scilicet, vi persecutionum; sed interior renovatur die et die; anima scilicet spe promissionum. Nam quod ad praesens, temporale et leve pressurae nostrae per supergressum in supergressum aeternum pondus gloriae perficit nobis, non intuentibus quae videntur, sed quae non videntur. Quae enim videntur, temporalia, de incommodis dicens; quae vero non videntur, aeterna, de praemiis spondens. Thessalonicensibus vero de vinculis scribens, utique beatos affirmavit,, quibus donatum esset non tantum credere in Christum, sed etiam pro ipso pati: Eumdem, inquit, agonem habentes quem in me vidistis, et nunc audistis. Nam et si libor super sacrificium, gaudeo et congaudeo omnibus vobis, perinde et vos gaudete et congaudete mihi. Vides quam martyrii definiat felicitatem, cui de gaudio mutuo acquirit solemnitatem. Ut proximus denique voti sui factus est, qualiter de prospectu ejus exsultans Timotheo scribit? Ego enim jam libor, et tempus dijunctionis instat. Agonem bonum decertavi, cursum consummavi, fidem custodivi; superest corona, quam mihi Dominus illa die reddet, scilicet passionis. Satis et ipse supra allocutus: Fidelis sermo: si enim commortui sumus Christo, et convivemus; si sufferimus, et conregnabimus; si negaverimus, et ille nos negabit; si non credimus, ille fidelis est, negare se non potest. Ne ergo confundaris martyrio Domini nostri, neque me vinctum ejus; quia praedixerat: Non enim dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed virtutis et dilectionis et sanae mentis. Virtute enim patimur ex dilectione in Deum, et sana mente, cum ob innocentiam patimur. Sed et sicubi tolerantiam praecipit, quibus magis eam quam passionibus prospicit? sicubi ab idololatria divellit, quid ei magis quam martyria praevellit?
pass_a_gloss: Paul, an Apostle, indeed, concerning a persecutor, who first shed the Church's blood, afterwards changing the sword to a stylus, and converting the machete into a plow; a rapacious wolf of Benjamin, then himself bringing food according to Jacob, in what way he commends martyrdoms, now already desirable to himself! when rejoicing about the Thessalonians: We glory, he says, in you in the Churches of God for your endurance and faith, in all the persecutions and pressures which you endure, a demonstration of the just judgment of God, so that you may be considered worthy of His kingdom, for which you also suffer. Just as also to the Romans: Not only, indeed, but also exulting in pressures; certain that pressure perfects endurance, endurance truly probation, probation indeed hope, hope indeed does not disappoint. And again: If we are sons, and heirs; heirs indeed of God, co-heirs truly of Christ: if we suffer, so that we may also be glorified with Him. I consider the passions of this time not to be worthy of the glory which will be revealed in us. And therefore afterwards: Who, he says, will separate us from the love of Christ? pressure, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or sword, according to what is written: we are killed all day for Your sake, we are considered as sheep for slaughter; but in all these things we overcome on account of Him who loved us. For we are persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor virtue, nor height, nor depth, nor any other condition will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. But also to the Corinthians, enumerating his own passions, he certainly defined suffering: In labors more abundantly, in prisons more frequently, in deaths often; from the Jews I received forty lashes minus one five times, three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, and the rest. Which if they seem more inconveniences than martyrdoms, nevertheless again: On account of which, he says, I consider it good in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ. Also in the preceding: Who are troubled in all things, but not constrained; and we are needy, but not extremely needy; since we are persecuted, but not abandoned; who are cast down, but not perishing: always carrying the mortification of Christ Jesus in our body. But if, he says, our outer man is corrupted, namely the flesh, by the power of persecutions; but the inner man is renewed day by day; namely the soul by the hope of promises. For what is present, temporal and light, our pressure, through surpassing, surpassing into eternal weight of glory perfects for us, not looking at what is seen, but what is not seen. For what is seen is temporal, speaking about inconveniences; what is not seen is eternal, promising about rewards. To the Thessalonians, indeed, writing about chains, he certainly affirmed the blessed ones, to whom it was given not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for Him: Having the same struggle which you saw in me and now hear. For even if I rejoice over sacrifice, I rejoice and congratulate all of you, and you rejoice and congratulate me in like manner. You see how he defines the happiness of martyrdom, by which he acquires solemnity from mutual joy. So that, having become next to his own wish, he writes to Timothy, exulting about his prospect? For I am already being poured out, and the time of departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; there remains a crown, which the Lord will give me on that day, namely of passion. Having spoken sufficiently above: Faithful is the word: if we have died with Christ, and live with Him; if we suffer, and reign with Him; if we deny, and He denies us; if we do not believe, He is faithful, He cannot deny Himself. So do not be ashamed of the martyrdom of our Lord, nor of me being bound by Him; because He predicted: For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power and love and a sound mind. For we suffer with power from love for God, and with a sound mind, when we suffer for innocence. But also where he commands endurance, to whom does he foresee it more than for martyrdoms? where he tears away from idolatry, what does he tear away more than martyrdoms?

pass_b_english: Paul the Apostle, once a persecutor who first shed the Church's blood, later exchanged the sword for a stylus and converted the machete into a plow; a rapacious wolf of Benjamin, then himself bringing food according to Jacob — in what way he commends martyrdoms, now already desirable to himself! When he rejoices over the Thessalonians: 'We glory in you in the Churches of God for your endurance and faith, in all the persecutions and pressures which you endure, a demonstration of the just judgment of God, so that you may be considered worthy of His kingdom, for which you also suffer' (2 Thess 1:4-5). Just as also to the Romans: 'Not only that, but we also exult in pressures; certain that pressure perfects endurance, endurance proves character, character produces hope, and hope does not disappoint' (Rom 5:3-5). And again: 'If we are sons, and heirs; heirs indeed of God, co-heirs of Christ: if we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified with Him' (Rom 8:17). 'I consider the passions of this time not to be worthy of the glory which will be revealed in us' (Rom 8:18). And therefore afterwards: 'Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Pressure, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or sword, according to what is written: For Your sake we are killed all day long; we are considered as sheep for slaughter; but in all these things we overcome through Him who loved us' (Rom 8:35-37). 'For we are persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor virtue, nor height, nor depth, nor any other condition will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord' (Rom 8:38-39). But also to the Corinthians, enumerating his own passions, he certainly defined suffering: 'In labors more abundantly, in prisons more frequently, in deaths often; from the Jews I received forty lashes minus one five times, three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, and the rest' (2 Cor 11:23-25). Which if they seem more inconveniences than martyrdoms, nevertheless again: 'On account of which I consider it good in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ' (2 Cor 12:10). Also in the preceding: 'We are troubled in all things, but not constrained; and we are needy, but not extremely needy; since we are persecuted, but not abandoned; we are cast down, but not perishing: always carrying the mortification of Christ Jesus in our body' (2 Cor 4:8-10). 'But if our outer man is corrupted, namely the flesh, by the power of persecutions; but the inner man is renewed day by day; namely the soul by the hope of promises' (2 Cor 4:16). 'For what is present, temporal and light, our pressure, through surpassing into surpassing, works for us an eternal weight of glory, not looking at what is seen, but what is not seen. For what is seen is temporal, speaking about inconveniences; what is not seen is eternal, promising about rewards' (2 Cor 4:17-18). To the Thessalonians, indeed, writing about chains, he certainly affirmed the blessed ones, to whom it was given not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer for Him: 'Having the same struggle which you saw in me and now hear' (Phil 1:30). 'For even if I am being poured out as a libation upon the sacrifice, I rejoice and congratulate all of you, and you rejoice and congratulate me in like manner' (Phil 2:17-18). You see how he defines the happiness of martyrdom, by which he acquires solemnity from mutual joy. So that, having become next to his own wish, he writes to Timothy, exulting about his prospect? 'For I am already being poured out, and the time of departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; there remains a crown, which the Lord will give me on that day, namely of passion' (2 Tim 4:6-8). Having spoken sufficiently above: 'Faithful is the word: if we have died with Christ, and live with Him; if we suffer, and reign with Him; if we deny, and He denies us; if we do not believe, He is faithful, He cannot deny Himself' (2 Tim 2:11-13). 'So do not be ashamed of the martyrdom of our Lord, nor of me being bound by Him; because He predicted: For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power and love and a sound mind' (2 Tim 1:7-8). 'For we suffer with power from love for God, and with a sound mind, when we suffer for innocence.' But also where he commands endurance, to whom does he foresee it more than for martyrdoms? Where he tears away from idolatry, what does he tear away more than martyrdoms?
